newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia government looks to budget for polls boost.
newsitem.headline: Australia government looks to budget for polls boost.

text.p: Australia's conservative government is looking to its mid-term budget on Tuesday to help restore its standing with voters and counter a growing threat from populist right-winger Pauline Hanson.

After last year's stringent budget that slashed spending by A$7 billion (US$5.5 billion) and sparked violent street protests, economists expect mild cuts and incentives for the government's key constituencies as an economic upturn reduces the pressure on finances.
Prime Minister John Howard has pledged the budget for the fiscal year from July will help create jobs, boost small business and foster development in rural areas.
But the big carrot to woo back voters, who Howard concedes are feeling ignored by his government, is expected to be a tax rebate scheme to encourage private sector savings.

The former Labor government budgeted A$1 billion for its own savings scheme in 1997/98, rising eventually to A$4.5 billion a year, but that plan was dumped after the Liberal-National coalition ousted Labor in a landslide win in March, 1996.
Howard's government has promised to come up with its own plan to put that money back in the pockets of the mainstream Australians who voted it into power.
Treasurer Peter Costello, while declaring the government remained well on target to wipe out the deficit, acknowledged the administration had no quick fix for stubborn joblessness.
On Sunday, Costello for the first time formally abandoned the government's target of 8.5 percent unemployment by the end of June, 1997.
"(But) I can promise you this, it'll be much better by June of 1998," he said in a television interview.
Unemployment was 8.7 percent in April and has remained stubbornly above 8.5 percent since the government won office.
The government is expected to spend big in this budget to help create jobs ahead of elections expected in late 1998 or early 1999.

It is also tipped to offer cash bonuses to older people to keep working instead of claiming pensions, continue a range of business aid programmes to help create jobs and focus a new A$1.25 billion environmental fund on job creation.
Economists said the government was well ahead of its target to balance the underlying budget -- which excludes windfalls such as asset sales -- in 1998/99.
They say the economy is growing faster than the government's projected 3.5 percent, in turn swelling government revenue.

Economists expect Costello to cut spending about A$2 billion to achieve a A$1.9 billion deficit in 1997/98 and possibly a small surplus the next year. The government has forecast, before any further savings announced on Tuesday, an underlying deficit of A$3.9 billion in 1997/98 and A$2.2 billion in 1998/99.
Costello's second budget has so far not sparked the wave of violent protests that greeted the first conservative budget.

But barely 18 months from the next election, Prime Minister John Howard's administration is in its worst position electorally since winning office as disaffected voters flock to Hanson's new One Nation Party.
The government has led Labor by 12 to 18 percentage points for most of its term, but the gap has been slashed to six points over recent weeks as support shifted to Hanson.
Reliable polls put support for Hanson's One Nation Party around 10 percent -- sparking speculation it is on the way to becoming the third force in Australian politics.

Hanson sparked a divisive race row last year with a speech to parliament warning that Asians threatened to swamp Australia and complained that Aborigines were receiving unfair treatment from the government at the expense of whites.
